title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

items.title: Ten days on, Boston Scientific still is not making product — and the breach never reached a controller
items.content_text: Ten days after detecting an intrusion on 25 August, Boston Scientific still has no full restoration date. Manufacturing, order processing and global shipping remain disrupted, with EDI and GHX orders queuing unfulfilled and production shifts cancelled at Irish plants. The company’s latest update reports no signs of malicious activity since detection and confines the unauthorised access to certain on-premise systems, with cloud services unaffected; implanted cardiac devices and established remote monitoring keep working. No entry route, vulnerability or ransomware involvement has been named, and no group has credibly claimed it. For OT defenders that absence is the point. Nothing here reached a PLC. A compromise of the enterprise systems that tell a plant what to build, where the material sits and where to ship it has halted production for a fortnight — the outcome most OT risk registers still file under IT.

items.title: The water campaign, quantified: CISA counts 100-plus internet-exposed systems hit, with controller logic and alarms altered
items.content_text: CISA has put a figure on July’s campaign against US water utilities: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, with reporting placing targeting across at least a dozen. Some degraded operations — lost pressure, flooding, plants run by hand — though supply was not widely interrupted, and in several intrusions actors altered controllers to disable shutdown processes and alarms, letting unsafe conditions develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. It stays on the page five weeks on because of the admission behind the number: the exposure that carried it was in nobody’s asset register.

items.title: Attackers walked from a wind farm’s firewall to another plant’s PLCs across a shared cellular APN — and stopped a turbine
items.content_text: CERT Polska’s follow-up report on attacks against Poland’s energy sector documents an intrusion path that maps almost exactly onto the exposure CISA and the NCSC are now warning about, and it is the reason this older item belongs on the page. Attackers compromised a FortiGate firewall at a wind farm, moved to a Teltonika cellular router, and then crossed a private cellular APN that had been provisioned without client isolation — meaning every SIM on that APN could reach every other. On the far side sat a WAGO PFC200 at a separate combined heat and power plant, still carrying default administrator credentials, which the attackers used to build an SSH bridge into the OT network. From there they forced three Siemens PLCs into STOP and set password protection on them, shutting down a steam turbine and the process-water treatment serving a town of roughly 50,000 people. CERT Polska assesses this as the first documented real-world OT intrusion via lateral movement across a private APN, and notes the shared-APN-without-isolation configuration is common in Poland and likely well beyond it.
tags: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, energy; first documented private-APN pivot

items.title: A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
items.content_text: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable.

items.title: A water-sector PLC maker was ransomed, and roughly 200 of its SCADA systems are reachable from the internet
items.content_text: Micro-Comm of Olathe, Kansas — which builds programmable logic controllers and the SCADAview CSX platform used by water and wastewater utilities — discovered a breach on 31 July and confirmed it publicly on 26 August, with the FBI investigating. The Barracuda ransomware group, a profit-motivated crew that says it is not state sponsored, published what it claims are nearly 850,000 stolen files totalling about 644 GB. Researchers reviewing the file listing report references to municipal customers, a US military facility, employee names and product documentation including system diagrams. The FBI has told the company it assesses the intrusion as opportunistic rather than targeted, and no manipulation of any customer’s control system has been reported. The number that should hold a water operator’s attention is a separate one: roughly 200 SCADAview CSX systems across US states are reachable from the public internet — the same exposure pattern that carried July’s campaign into more than 100 water systems.

items.title: NCSC: OT targeting is up across sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre published a statement on 27 August saying it is seeing increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors worldwide, including in the UK, carried out by a range of threat actors, and that this has already produced limited real-world disruption. The agency ties it to a broader pattern of disruptive activity against internet-exposed systems and edge devices — routers, gateways and firewalls that hand an attacker a foothold. Its asks are concrete: keep an accurate inventory of internet-facing systems, understand what each edge device does and where its data flows, patch promptly, retire end-of-life equipment, disable Telnet and SNMP v1/v2, and watch for unexpected configuration changes or outbound connections. Coming a day after CISA’s exposure guidance, this is two national agencies independently reaching the same conclusion in the same week.
tags: Agency warning — Cross-sector OT targeting, real-world disruption

items.title: The cheapest way to black out a grid may be to desynchronise the batteries holding it steady
items.content_text: A report published on 3 September by Centrii models coordinated attacks on grid-scale battery energy storage using a Monte Carlo simulation run 10,000 times across three security postures. Its headline figure — a 92% probability of a major attack on Great Britain’s battery fleet by 2031 under today’s average posture, falling to 61% under mandatory IEC 62443 certification — is a modelled projection, not an observation, and it comes from a vendor that sells risk quantification. The mechanism underneath it deserves attention on its own merits. BESS fleets are increasingly commanded through cloud platforms that address thousands of units at once. An attacker does not need to damage a battery or stop generation; synchronising charge and discharge commands, or inserting a few seconds of delay into frequency response, turns the grid’s stabiliser into an amplifier. Protective relays then trip in sequence, and the report models cascade to blackout inside two minutes. The author estimates roughly 29% of GB capacity, or 5.4% of ERCOT’s fleet, would suffice.
tags: Research — Quantified risk modelling; grid-scale battery storage and the cloud control layer

items.title: A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC.
tags: Forescout Vedere Labs — AI-assisted exploit development against PLCs

items.title: CISA red-teamed two critical-infrastructure organisations to domain admin — one SOC caught it, the other saw nothing at all
items.content_text: CISA’s advisory AA26-237A, published 25 August and still circulating in OT discussion a week later, reports two authorised red-team assessments run against critical-infrastructure operators — one a government services and facilities organisation, the other a water and wastewater utility. Both were fully compromised at the domain level, and in both the team went on to reach sensitive business systems and cloud resources. The interesting part is the divergence in detection, which is why the advisory is titled around two security operations centres rather than two intrusions. At the first organisation the team gained initial access to several workstations, escalated to domain-wide privileges and moved laterally to business systems and cloud resources without being detected. At the second, defenders spotted the initial compromise quickly and quarantined the affected hosts. CISA’s conclusion is uncomfortable for anyone building a business case around tooling: spend was not the variable that separated the two outcomes. Analysts who understood the environment, knew what normal looked like, and could act without waiting on another team were. The advisory presses operators to establish behavioural baselines, tune monitoring to them, and remove the organisational friction that turns a detected alert into an unactioned one.

items.title: Fire Ant moved up a layer: the routers and TACACS servers your OT quietly trusts are now the objective
items.content_text: Sygnia published incident-response findings on 31 August showing that the espionage actor it tracks as Fire Ant — assessed as substantially mirroring the China-nexus cluster reported elsewhere as UNC3886 — has expanded beyond hypervisor compromise into what the firm calls the trusted infrastructure layer. In the intrusions Sygnia investigated, the actor compromised Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts, then used them as operating platforms for traffic collection, credential theft and long-term persistence, explicitly in order to reach connected high-value environments including critical infrastructure. The tooling included Medusa rootkit components, custom SSH backdoors, malware masquerading as Zabbix monitoring agents and packet-triggered backdoors, some dating to 2025 and reused this year. The detail OT teams should sit with is the anti-forensics: the actor suppressed router logging, altered command output so operators saw a clean device, and tampered with host logs, meaning no single telemetry source could reconstruct the intrusion. No manipulation of a physical process has been reported — this is pre-positioning in the control plane that OT depends on.
tags: Threat research — Sygnia; China-nexus actor targeting network and authentication infrastructure

items.title: CISA put SonicWall’s exploited SMA1000 pair in KEV a day after disclosure — a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw chained to code execution
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance have been exploited in the wild, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2 September as part of a seven-CVE batch. CVE-2026-83548, carrying a CVSS score of 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker reach sensitive functionality; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an OS command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console that an authenticated attacker can turn into remote code execution. SonicWall says it observed exploitation of both, which points to the pair being chained for unauthenticated code execution on the appliance. The vendor found the flaws and the attacks internally, and has published no indicators of compromise. Models 6210, 7210 and 8200v are affected. For OT operators this is the exact class of device that vendor engineers, integrators and on-call staff use to reach the plant from outside — a box that sits at the boundary, terminates trusted sessions and is rarely covered by an OT change window.
tags: SonicWall SMA1000 — Two zero-days exploited, CVSS 10 chain, now in CISA KEV

items.title: CISA’s 3 September batch lands on the remote-access client itself — a CVSS 9.6 root-level flaw in IXON VPN
items.content_text: The five advisories CISA published on 3 September are worth reading in a particular order, because the first one sits on the exact attack path two national agencies spent last week warning about. ICSA-26-246-02 covers CVE-2026-75925 in the IXON VPN Client below 1.4.7, rated CVSS v3.1 9.6: the client’s local configuration interface accepts changes without authenticating the requester, and does not neutralise line-ending sequences before writing them to a file that a privileged subprocess later consumes — so an attacker can inject extra directives and have commands run as root or SYSTEM. The injected configuration survives reboots, and the VPN keeps working normally, so nothing about the machine’s behaviour tells the engineer using it that anything changed. This is the software sitting on maintenance laptops and engineering workstations that reach machines in the field. The rest of the batch is more routine but not trivial: ICSA-26-246-06 flags CVE-2026-77393 in Inductive Automation Ignition 8.1.53 and earlier at CVSS 8.8, where the Gateway’s Create Project Role(s) setting shipped blank and any authenticated user able to run gateway scripts can create projects; ICSA-26-246-03 covers CVE-2026-12663 in Rockwell ControlFLASH 15.07 and earlier, whose installer granted the Everyone group write access to a product directory; ICSA-26-246-01 covers CVE-2026-77477 in the OPC Foundation UA LocalDiscoveryServer installers; and ICSA-26-246-08 covers a missing-authorization issue, CVE-2026-82684, in Tycon Systems TPDIN-Monitor-WEB3 2.2.9 and earlier that could expose credentials, configuration or flash contents.

items.title: CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
items.content_text: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04). Rockwell’s own round-up, reported 2 September, puts the total above a dozen fixes and adds detail the CISA summaries do not: remote code execution in FactoryTalk Historian, privilege escalation in FactoryTalk Activation Manager and in the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool, arbitrary code execution through the ControlFLASH firmware utility, cross-site scripting plus a web-server denial of service in ArmorStart distributed motor controllers, and further denial-of-service issues in 1756-ENBT and in Logix controllers via a third-party component. One item needs care rather than alarm: Rockwell’s advisory for CVE-2026-9637, a high-severity denial of service in ControlLogix and CompactLogix, is flagged as exploited in its document header but listed as not exploited in the body, and CISA states it is not aware of exploitation — read it as a documentation inconsistency, not a live campaign, and patch it on its merits.

items.title: Cisco patches root-level flaws in the routers and switches that OT quietly depends on
items.content_text: Cisco released fixes on 3 September covering seven CVEs in IOS XR, two of which — CVE-2026-20274 and CVE-2026-20279 — carry a CVSS score of 9.8, plus a third at the same score, CVE-2026-20212, in Nexus 9000 series switches. The reported condition is the kind that removes every intermediate step from an attack chain: a remote, unauthenticated attacker can reach TCP ports that listen by default and execute code with root privileges. None of this is OT equipment in the ISA-95 sense, and none of it will arrive through an ICS advisory feed. It is, however, the layer that carries plant traffic to the data centre, terminates the site-to-site links between facilities, and in a great many networks enforces the segmentation that the whole OT security programme is resting on. That makes it the practical companion to the Fire Ant research elsewhere on this page, which documents a China-nexus actor operating from compromised Cisco IOS XR routers and TACACS servers precisely because they sit outside OT monitoring.

items.title: Britain moves to take the power to disconnect your suppliers — and a four-day generator outage is what tabled the amendment
items.content_text: Late amendments to the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would give ministers power to stop critical-sector organisations using technology suppliers judged high risk. The Bill was introduced in November 2025, has cleared the Commons and sits in the Lords as HL Bill 32, close to Royal Assent; the amendments were tabled on 24 August, two days after reporting that Iran-linked actors had forced a small UK generating site offline for four days (see Incidents & Attacks). The approach is a departure worth noting: rather than only demanding better in-house security from operators, it lets government cut them off from third parties it considers inadequately secured, regardless of the supplier’s size or sector. The Bill already carries strict incident-reporting timelines and heavy penalties. Practitioners quoted in the coverage make the obvious point — a small integrator or managed service provider with standing remote access into a plant may not think of itself as critical national infrastructure, but a designation regime will decide that for it.

items.title: Washington has declared the grid’s supply chain a national emergency — and the order names PLCs and RTUs explicitly
items.content_text: Executive Order 14420, signed on 26 August, declares a national emergency over foreign-supplied equipment in the US bulk-power system and prohibits acquiring, importing, transferring or installing covered equipment sourced from designated foreign adversaries. Scope is drawn at transmission rated 69 kV and above, expressly excluding local distribution. What makes it an OT item rather than a trade item is the equipment list: alongside transformers, inverters and storage systems it names industrial control systems — remote terminal units, programmable logic controllers and safety systems — and reaches the operating software and firmware embedded in them, on the stated concern of hidden backdoors and unauthorised remote control. The order also directs the Department of Energy to identify equipment already installed that raises the same concern and to recommend mitigations, which may include isolation, enhanced monitoring or replacement. Prohibiting rules are expected from DOE within 120 days, so the operative detail is still to come.

items.title: The Coast Guard now has one office that owns maritime cyber policy — expect the inspection questions to sharpen
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard has stood up an Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy (CG‑MCP) as the central authority for the cyber safety and security of the Marine Transportation System — roughly 360 commercial sea and river ports, plus vessels and regulated facilities. Created under the Director of Inspections and Compliance, it will develop domestic policy, contribute to international standards, direct a coordinated cybersecurity compliance and enforcement strategy, act as the primary liaison to industry and other agencies, and monitor emerging technology. The service framed it around the problem every sector has: information and operational technology are delivering real efficiency across the MTS while enlarging the risk to a critical infrastructure sector. It arrives roughly eighteen months after a February 2025 GAO report faulted the Coast Guard’s cyber incident data quality, access to inspection deficiency records, strategy alignment, and competency requirements for staff with MTS cyber responsibilities; the service did not say the office was a direct response.

items.title: A six-month federal pilot will red-team Texas water utilities — and it is meant to become a template
items.content_text: The White House Office of the National Cyber Director, the EPA, CISA and Texas Cyber Command launched Project Watershed 250 on 31 August, a six-month pilot that will stress-test water utility networks in Texas with red-team exercises and provide participating systems with federal, state and vendor-supplied cyber defences at no cost. Microsoft, Palo Alto Networks, Dragos, Tenable, Forescout and Reflection AI are named among the participants. The administration says the pilot is not a response to the July intrusions that affected more than 30 Minnesota water systems, though it acknowledges those incidents underscored the exposure; officials frame it as a scalable model to extend nationally if it works. The reason this matters beyond Texas is the design assumption behind it, stated plainly by the participants: the sector’s roughly 150,000 systems are mostly small, thinly staffed and cannot be turned into enterprise security organisations, so the intervention has to be visibility and prioritisation delivered from outside rather than headcount hired inside. Whatever the pilot publishes about what the red teams actually found will be the more valuable output — CISA’s own red-team assessments at two critical-infrastructure organisations, released a week earlier, showed one failing to detect initial access and lateral movement entirely.

items.title: In one week, anyone selling a connected product into the EU owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act enters its reporting phase on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process.

items.title: “Prepare to disconnect” is now written guidance — and it assumes you can run the plant for months without IT
items.content_text: The Five Eyes agencies’ CI Fortify — Advice for isolating vital systems, published 28 July and pushed back into the OT conversation on 2 September by vendor analyses from Nozomi, OPSWAT and Zscaler, sets out a six-step path to being able to cut vital OT loose from everything else and keep delivering service. The steps are unglamorous and in order: identify vital systems and networks; identify your critical customers and set a service target in real units — megawatts, million gallons per day; group hosts by criticality and trust; map every interconnection and pick your isolation points; build separation that actually holds; then write and test a graduated isolation plan. The part practitioners keep returning to is the dependency list. The guidance names the shared services that quietly defeat isolation — Active Directory, DNS and DHCP, PKI and certificate services, NTP/PTP time sync, shared hypervisors and SANs, backup and recovery, and the routing and switching fabric itself — and says operators must eliminate those dependencies, not document them. It is blunt about carrier links too: treat any carrier-provided service as untrusted and potentially hostile, encrypt with a dedicated device rather than the crypto built into an OT product, and manage that device only from inside the OT domain. That advice reads differently after CERT Polska’s private-APN case (see Incidents & Attacks), which is the failure mode this paragraph exists to prevent.
